title: Last Stone Weight
description: You are given an array of integers stones where stones[i] is the weight of the ith stone. On each turn, choose the two heaviest stones and smash them together. Suppose the heaviest two stones have weights x and y with x <= y. If x == y, both stones are destroyed. If x != y, the stone of weight x is destroyed and the stone of weight y keeps weight y - x. At the end of the game, at most one stone remains. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remains.

examples.explanation: Combine 8 and 7 to get 1, leaving [2,4,1,1,1]; combine 4 and 2 to get 2, leaving [2,1,1,1]; combine 2 and 1 to get 1, leaving [1,1,1]; combine 1 and 1 to destroy both, leaving [1].
There is only one stone, so it remains with weight 1.

hints: You always need the two heaviest stones quickly.
A max-heap returns the largest element in O(log n) per operation.
Smashing the two heaviest either destroys both or leaves their difference, which goes back on the heap.

title: Maximum Product of Two Elements in an Array
description: Given the array of integers nums, choose two different indices i and j such that the value of (nums[i] - 1) * (nums[j] - 1) is maximized. Return the maximum value.

examples.explanation: The maximum is (5 - 1) * (4 - 1) = 12.
The maximum is (5 - 1) * (5 - 1) = 16, using the two 5s.

hints: The product is maximized by the two largest elements of the array.
A max-heap gives the largest elements first; you only need the top two.
Subtract 1 from each of the two values before multiplying.

title: Take Gifts From the Richest Pile
description: You are given an integer array gifts denoting the number of gifts in various piles, and an integer k. For each of k seconds, do the following: choose the pile with the maximum number of gifts (if several piles tie for the maximum, choose any one of them), and leave behind floor(sqrt(x)) gifts in that pile, where x was its number of gifts before that second. Return the total number of gifts remaining after k seconds.

examples.explanation: Second 1: pile 100 becomes 10. Second 2: pile 64 becomes 8. Second 3: pile 25 becomes 5. Second 4: pile 10 becomes 3. Remaining: 5 + 8 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 29.
Each pile of 1 becomes floor(sqrt(1)) = 1, so nothing changes and 4 gifts remain.

hints: Every second you need the current maximum pile.
A max-heap supports extract-max and reinsert in O(log n).
Shrink a pile with the integer (floor) square root.

title: The K Weakest Rows in a Matrix
description: You are given an m x n binary matrix mat of 1s (soldiers) and 0s (civilians). In each row, all the 1s come before all the 0s. Row i is weaker than row j if row i has fewer soldiers than row j, or the same number of soldiers and i < j. Return the indices of the k weakest rows, ordered from weakest to strongest. Ties are always broken by the smaller row index.

examples.explanation: Soldier counts are [2,4,1,2,5]. The 3 weakest rows are 2 (1 soldier), then 0 and 3 (2 soldiers each, smaller index first).
Soldier counts are [1,4,1,1]. The 2 weakest rows are 0 and 2.

hints: Count the soldiers in each row first.
Sort the rows by (soldier count, row index), or push those pairs into a min-heap.
The first k entries of that order are the answer.

title: Final Array State After K Multiplication Operations I
description: You are given an integer array nums, an integer k, and an integer multiplier. Perform k operations: in each operation, find the minimum value x in nums; if the minimum occurs multiple times, choose the occurrence with the smallest index; then replace that occurrence with x * multiplier. Return the state of nums after all k operations. Equal minimums are always resolved by choosing the smallest index.

examples.explanation: The operations pick indices 1, 0, 2, 1, 0 in order, giving [8,4,6,5,6].
The operations pick index 0, then 1, then 0, giving [16,8].

hints: Each operation needs the current minimum and its index.
A min-heap of (value, index) pairs breaks ties by the smaller index automatically.
Multiply the popped value and push the updated pair back.

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
description: You are given an integer k and an initial array nums. Then values arrive one by one from an array adds. After inserting each value of adds into the collection of all values seen so far (the initial nums plus every inserted value), record the current kth largest value. Return all recorded values in order, one per value in adds.

examples.explanation: After inserting 3 the 3rd largest is 4; after 5 it is 5; after 10 it is 5; after 9 it is 8; after 4 it is 8.
With k = 1 the recorded value is always the maximum so far: -3, -2, -2, 0, 4.

hints: You only ever need the k largest values seen so far.
A min-heap of size k keeps the kth largest at its top.
Insert each new value, shrink the heap back to size k if needed, then read the top.

title: Minimum Number Game
description: You are given a 0-indexed integer array nums of even length. Alice and Bob play rounds until nums is empty. In each round: Alice removes the minimum element of nums, then Bob removes the minimum of the remaining elements; Bob appends his removed element, followed by Alice's removed element, to an array arr. Return arr after all rounds.

examples.explanation: Round 1: Alice removes 2, Bob removes 3, arr = [3,2]. Round 2: Alice removes 4, Bob removes 5, arr = [3,2,5,4].
Alice removes 2, Bob removes 5, arr = [5,2].

hints: Each round removes the two smallest remaining elements.
A min-heap yields them in order: first Alice's, then Bob's.
Append Bob's element before Alice's element.

title: Find Subsequence of Length K With the Largest Sum
description: You are given an integer array nums and an integer k. Find a subsequence of nums of length k with the largest possible sum, and return its elements in their original relative order. (A subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous.)

examples.explanation: The largest-sum subsequence of length 3 is [2,3,3].
The largest-sum subsequence of length 3 is [-1,3,4].
The largest-sum subsequence of length 2 is [3,4].

hints: First pick the k largest values; a max-heap helps.
Keep track of each chosen element's original index.
Sort the chosen indices to restore the original relative order.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array. Note that it is the kth largest element in sorted order, not the kth distinct element.

examples.explanation: Sorted descending: [6,5,4,3,2,1]; the 2nd largest is 5.
Sorted descending: [6,5,5,4,3,3,2,2,1]; the 4th largest is 4.

hints: A min-heap of size k holds the k largest elements seen so far.
Push each element; if the heap grows past size k, pop the smallest.
After one pass, the heap top is the kth largest.

title: Task Scheduler
description: You are given an array of CPU tasks labeled with uppercase letters A through Z, and a non-negative integer n. Each task takes one unit of time, and in each unit you may run one task or stay idle. Two identical tasks must be separated by at least n other time units. Return the minimum number of time units needed to finish all tasks.

examples.explanation: One optimal schedule is A -> B -> idle -> A -> B -> idle -> A -> B, taking 8 units.
No cooldown is needed, so 6 units suffice.

constraints: tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter

hiddenTests.input:
[A, A, A, A, A, A, B, C, D, E, F, G]
2

hints: Always run the available task with the most remaining instances.
A max-heap of remaining counts models that greedy choice.
Simulate in rounds of n + 1 slots, adding idle time only while tasks remain.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
description: You are given a 2D array lists where each row lists[i] is a sorted integer array in non-decreasing order. A row may be empty, and there is at least one row. Merge all rows into a single sorted linked list and return its head. Represent an empty result as an empty list.

examples.explanation: Merging all rows in order gives [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6].
The only row is empty, so the merged list is empty.

constraints: The total number of elements across all rows is at most 10^4
Each row is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Seed a min-heap with the first element of every non-empty row.
Repeatedly pop the smallest value, then push the next element from the same row.
Append each popped value to the merged linked list as you go.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
description: Given an array of points where points[i] = [xi, yi] is a point on the X-Y plane, and an integer k, return the k closest points to the origin (0, 0). Return the points sorted by distance ascending. When distances tie, order by the smaller x first, then by the smaller y. (Compare distances using xi^2 + yi^2 to avoid floating point.)

examples.explanation: The squared distances are 10 and 8; [-2,2] is closer.
The squared distances are 18, 26, 20; the two closest are [3,3] and [-2,4].

hints: Squared distance xi^2 + yi^2 is enough for comparisons.
A max-heap of size k keeps the k closest points seen so far.
Sort the final k points by (distance, x, y) to fix the required order.

title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
description: You are given two integer arrays nums1 and nums2, both sorted in non-decreasing order, and an integer k. Consider all pairs (u, v) where u is from nums1 and v is from nums2. Return the k pairs with the smallest sums. Order the pairs by pair sum ascending; when sums tie, the pair with the smaller first value comes first, then the pair with the smaller second value.

examples.explanation: The smallest sums are 3, 5, 7, giving [[1,2],[1,4],[1,6]].
The two smallest sums are both 2, giving [[1,1],[1,1]].
Only two pairs exist, so return both: [[1,3],[2,3]].

hints: The smallest pair is (nums1[0], nums2[0]).
From a popped pair (i, j), the next candidates are (i+1, j) and (i, j+1); use a visited set to avoid duplicates.
Order the heap by (sum, first value, second value) to match the required order.

title: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks
description: You have some sticks with positive integer lengths. You can connect any two sticks into a single stick; the cost of a connection is the sum of the two sticks' lengths. Return the minimum total cost to connect all sticks into one stick. If there is only one stick, the cost is 0.

examples.explanation: Connect 2 and 3 (cost 5), then connect 5 and 4 (cost 9); total 14.
Connect 1 and 3 (cost 4), connect 4 and 5 (cost 9), connect 9 and 8 (cost 17); total 30.

hints: Connecting the two shortest sticks first is always optimal.
A min-heap repeatedly yields the two shortest sticks.
Add their sum to the total cost and push the combined stick back.

title: Single-Threaded CPU
description: You are given a 2D array tasks where tasks[i] = [enqueueTime, processingTime] means the ith task becomes available at enqueueTime and needs processingTime units to finish. A single-threaded CPU processes tasks as follows: if it is idle and no task is available, it stays idle until the next task arrives; if it is idle and tasks are available, it picks the available task with the shortest processing time, breaking ties by the smaller original index; once started, a task runs to completion. Return the order in which the CPU processes the tasks, as their original indices.

examples.explanation: Task 0 runs from time 1 to 3; then task 2 (shortest available) runs 3 to 5; then task 3 runs 5 to 6; then task 1 runs 6 to 10.
All tasks are available at time 7, so they run in order of increasing processing time: [4,3,2,0,1].

hints: Sort the tasks by enqueue time while remembering original indices.
A min-heap keyed by (processing time, index) holds the available tasks.
When the heap is empty, jump the clock forward to the next arrival.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
description: You are given an integer array nums whose values are inserted one by one into a data structure. After each insertion, compute the median of all values inserted so far: for an odd count it is the middle value, for an even count it is the average of the two middle values. Return the medians in order, one per insertion.

examples.explanation: After inserting 1 the median is 1.0; after inserting 2 it is (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5.
The medians are 1.0, 1.5, 2.0.

hints: Keep the lower half of the values in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap.
Rebalance after each insertion so the heap sizes differ by at most one.
The median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of the two tops.

title: IPO
description: You are given k project opportunities. Project i yields profits[i] and requires at least capital[i] of current capital to start. You begin with capital w. Starting a project costs nothing beyond the requirement, and finishing it adds its profit to your capital. You may complete at most k distinct projects. Return the maximum final capital you can achieve.

examples.explanation: Start project 0 (capital 0, profit 1), then with capital 1 start project 2 (profit 3); final capital 4.
Start projects 0, 1, 2 in order; final capital 6.

hints: Sort the projects by required capital.
A max-heap of profits holds every project you can currently afford.
Each round, fund the affordable project with the largest profit and repeat.

title: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
description: You are given k integer arrays nums, each sorted in non-decreasing order. A range [a, b] covers the lists if every list contains at least one element within [a, b]. Return the smallest such range as [start, end], minimizing end - start. If several ranges tie for the smallest length, return the one with the smaller start.

examples.explanation: The range [20,24] covers all three lists and is the smallest possible.
The range [3,4] covers both lists with the smallest length.

constraints: Each list is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Seed a min-heap with the first element of each list and track the current maximum.
Each step advances the list holding the current minimum.
Record the best range seen; on a length tie keep the smaller start.

title: Reorganize String
description: Given a string s, rearrange its characters so that no two adjacent characters are the same. Produce the rearrangement using this deterministic method: count each character's frequency; if the highest frequency is greater than (n + 1) / 2 (integer division), return the empty string. Otherwise, order the distinct characters by decreasing frequency (ties broken by smaller character first), then write them into the result by filling even positions 0, 2, 4, ... first, followed by odd positions 1, 3, 5, .... Return the resulting string.

examples.explanation: Frequencies: a=2, b=1. Order [a, b]; evens get 'a','a', odd gets 'b' -> "aba".
Frequency of 'a' is 3 > (4 + 1) / 2 = 2, so no valid rearrangement exists.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: If one character appears more than half the time (rounded up), two copies must end up adjacent.
A max-heap by remaining frequency always tells you which character to place next.
Placing frequent characters at even indices first guarantees separation when a solution exists.

title: Maximum Performance of a Team
description: You are given n engineers with speed[i] and efficiency[i]. The performance of a team is the sum of its members' speeds multiplied by the minimum efficiency among its members. Choose a team of at most k engineers to maximize performance. Return the maximum performance modulo 10^9 + 7.

examples.explanation: Choose engineers 1 and 3 (0-indexed): speeds 10 + 5 = 15, min efficiency 4 -> 15 * 4 = 60.
Best team of up to 3 engineers achieves performance 68.

hints: Sort engineers by efficiency descending, so the current engineer is always the team's minimum efficiency.
As you sweep, keep the fastest engineers seen so far — but at most k of them.
A min-heap of speeds maintains the top-k speed sum while you consider each possible minimum efficiency.
